sections.heading: Theoretical and experimental investigation of a nonlinear compressive-mode energy harvester with high power output under weak excitations
sections.text:
Zhengbao Yang, Yang Zhu and Jean Zu

Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, M5 S 3G8, Canada

E-mail: zbyang@mie.utoronto.ca

Received 21 September 2014, revised 8 November 2014

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Harvesting ambient vibration energy is a promising method for realizing self-powered autonomous operation for low-power electronic devices. Most energy harvesters developed to date employ bending-beam configurations and work around the resonant points. There are two critical problems that have hindered the widespread adoption of energy harvesters: insufficient power output and narrow working bandwidth. To overcome these problems, we proposed a novel energy harvester, called a high-efficiency compressive-mode piezoelectric energy harvester (HC-PEH). The HC-PEH delicately synthesizes the merits of the force amplification effect of the flexural motion and the dynamic properties of elastic beams, and thus is capable of high power output with wide working bandwidth. In this paper, theoretical and experimental studies were performed on the HC-PEH. Taking nonlinear stiffness, nonlinear damping, and nonlinear piezoelectricity into account, we developed an analytical model that provides comprehensive insight into the nonlinear mechanical and electrical behaviors of the system. The analytical results closely render the experimental data and demonstrate great performance enhancement. In the experiment, a maximum power output of $5 4 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ is generated at $2 6 \mathrm { H z }$ under an acceleration of $4 . 9 \ \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 2 }$ , which is over one order of magnitude higher than other stateof-the-art systems.

Keywords: energy harvesting, piezoelectric, geometric nonlinearity, flextensional transducer, high power output

(Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
With the recent rapid advancements in wireless sensor networks and microelectronics, the need for long-life, efficient power sources has become increasingly pressing. A wireless sensor network, such as that used in, a forest fire monitoring system, usually spreads over thousands of miles with a large quantity of sensors. The replacement or maintenance of such a large number of batteries in remote areas is very costly and time-consuming. A microelectronic device, such as an artificial pacemaker, is embedded in a patientʼs chest. The replacement of the battery poses a severe threat to the patientʼs health and can even cause death in some cases. Therefore, new inexhaustible power sources that do not require regular recharging and maintenance are urgently needed to replace commonly used electrochemical batteries.

Harnessing ambient wasted energy and converting it to electricity is a feasible and popular approach to realize inexhaustible power supply for small devices. Mechanical vibration is an abundant energy source that is widely available in vehicles, buildings, bridges, and biological systems. Vibration energy can be harnessed using suitable mechanicalto-electrical energy transducers such as electrostatic, electromagnetic, magnetostrictive, or piezoelectric converting devices. Among them, piezoelectric transducers show superior conversion efficiency and outstanding simplicity. Moreover, piezoelectric transducers can be manufactured in both microand macroscale [1, 2], which makes them more adaptable in practical applications.

A conventional piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) is generally composed of a cantilever beam with piezoelectric materials bonded to its surface and a proof mass at the tip end. Most commercially available PEHs employ the cantilever structure. The benefits of the cantilever structure come from the simplicity, compactness, and high bending strain of the structure itself. However, the cantilevered energy harvester works efficiently only around the resonant point—that is, it cannot accommodate the random frequency-variant excitations in the ambient environment. Various approaches have been proposed to overcome the narrow bandwidth problem. Tuning the resonance frequency to match the excitation is a straightforward idea. Researchers [3–5] have succeeded in actively tuning the resonance frequencies of energy harvesting systems by applying electrical inputs. The active-feedback tuning method may work efficiently under random excitations. However, the method itself consumes a friction of electricity, which affects the overall power output. The multi beam method is another option for broadening the bandwidth. Since a cantilever has one resonant point, if an energy harvesting system is set up with multiple cantilevers with different resonant points, broad bandwidth is achieved. In [6–8], multi beam structures were proposed in different ways. They are all good methods of assembling cantilevered energy harvesters effectively, but they may not be favorable in light of cost and volume. From the viewpoint of the vibration behaviors, a nonlinear system has a much wider resonant spectrum than a linear one. Accordingly, introducing nonlinearity into an energy harvesting system becomes a possible way to broaden the working bandwidth [9–12]. Using a nonlinear magnetic field to induce nonlinearity is a commonly employed approach. However, it has certain limitations in some situations where nonmagnetic solutions are required, as in the case of MRI-compatible medical implants. Another approach is employing the intrinsic geometric nonlinearity that circumvents the problem in magnetic PEHs. The bi stable state in the vertical cantilever [13], the parametric resonance in the pendulum-lever structure [14], and the negative stiffness in the hair bundle structure [15] have been exploited to broaden the bandwidth to a higher level.

Low power output is another serious issue hampering the widespread adoption of energy harvesters. The amount of energy generated by PEHs is not sufficient to power most electronic devices [16, 17]. Examining various existing designs, we found that a majority of them work in the bending mode where piezoceramics bear the bending stress, such as the cantilever [18], the curved beam [19], and the fixed-fixed beam [20]. Piezoceramics can fatigue and fail easily under dynamic bending loads, and thus these PEHs do not show a satisfactory energy generation capability. In 2004, Deng [21] and Kim [22] proposed the idea of using the flextensional transducer in energy harvesting systems to improve efficiency and robustness, where piezoceramics work in the tensile mode. The flextensional PEH is typically composed of a piezoelectric disc sandwiched between two convex metal plates that amplify the induced force and enhance the mechanical strength. The flextensional PEHs are suitable for applications in large-force, high-frequency environments, but they cannot generate power efficiently under ambient weak excitations.

![](images/33c42a55855a60a28e4b1c1a58961e65a78fbe1c38ed783abc40258de0137f48.jpg)  
Figure 1. Schematic diagram of the HC-PEH. Vibrational states are shown in translucence.

Inspired by the geometric nonlinearity and flextensional PEHs, we proposed a novel energy harvester, which we called a high-efficiency compressive-mode piezoelectric energy harvester (HC-PEH). The HC-PEH overcomes the problem of low power output in exiting PEHs and simultaneously broadens the working bandwidth. Given the characteristics of piezoceramics (strength is superior but toughness is unsatisfactory), a novel multistage force-amplification mechanism was developed in the HC-PEH to achieve high efficiency. Furthermore, the HC-PEH takes full advantage of the low stiffness of bending beams, and thus fulfills the goal of broad working bandwidth in low-frequency spectra. An analytical model was developed to investigate the nonlinear dynamic responses and the effects of nonlinear damping, nonlinear stiffness, and nonlinear piezoelectricity on performance. The analytical results and the experimental data are matched very well and indicate a significant performance enhancement. Compared with other state-of-the-art systems, the HC-PEH can generate electricity one order of magnitude higher under the same conditions.

The content of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we discuss the strategy of the design. A finite element analysis is conducted to optimize the configuration. Section 3 articulates the modeling methodology of the nonlinear electromechanical system. The developed model is solved analytically using the harmonic balance method. Section 4 presents the fabricated prototype and the experimental procedure. Results and discussions are given in section 5. The summary is concluded in section 6.

sections.heading: 2. Design
sections.text:
The configuration of the proposed HC-PEH is shown in figure 1. The HC-PEH is supported by two horizontally laid elastic beams bonded to the base. The piezoelectric element is set in the center, sandwiched between two bow-shaped plates, which is called the flex-compressive center in this study. A pair of mass blocks are added to the system to adjust the working frequency range and to capture more inertial energy. Figure 2 illustrates the force transmission process. While working, a base vibration is first transferred through the elastic beams and absorbed by the proof masses and the flexcompressive center. Then the vertical vibration of the center induces longitudinal stress along the elastic beam. The longitudinal motion is further transferred to become the flexural motion of the bow-shaped plate, and thus causes compressive stress in the piezo plate. As a result of the piezoelectric effect, the stress in the piezoelectric materials finally results in the electric displacement. In the mechanicalto-electrical energy conversion process, the excitation is amplified twice: first by the elastic beam from the vertical vibration of the proof mass to the horizontal stretch of the elastic beam, and second by the bow-shaped plate from the horizontal stretch of the elastic beam to the vertical compression in the piezo plate. The HC-PEH proposed here is a two-stage amplification structure that can be easily expanded to a multistage amplification structure by coupling more flexcompressive centers in different ways.

![](images/3b4af346b910fb67fc4a571f5546e150c19d8da41364d3d9d5e65d92ef45afc5.jpg)  
Figure 2. Flow chart of the force transmission process in the HC-PEH.

The piezoelectric element in the HC-PEH works in the compressive mode—that is, the active material experiences a dynamic compressive load while operating. It is known that the compressive strength is commensurate with the tensile strength for general metal materials. However, there exists a considerable difference for ceramics, which are weak in tension but strong in compression; in fact, their compressive strength is about 10 times larger than their tensile strength. The static compressive strength of piezoceramic materials from PI Ceramic can be larger than $6 0 0 \mathrm { M p a }$ , while the tensile strength is limited to $5 \mathrm {- } 1 0 \%$ of the compressive load limit. Piezoceramics also crack easily under dynamic bending stress. The compressive mode is therefore preferred to other modes in terms of reliability.

The flex-compressive center is composed of one piezoelectric plate and two bow-shaped concave metal plates. The bow-shaped plate serves as a mechanical transformer, translating the incident normal tensile strain into a lateral compressive strain. It also acts as an amplifier, maximizing the small incident normal load force induced by vibration into a large lateral acting force in the piezoelectric element. The flex-compressive transducer may have rectangular or discshaped profiles that ought to be determined by working conditions and output power requirements. Although the disc is the most common configuration [22, 23], the rectangular configuration is adopted in our experiment because we found that there is a periodic unwanted circumferential stress in the metal end-caps for circular transducers, as shown in figure 3. The circumferential stress consumes a fraction of the absorbed mechanical energy and impacts the overall effectiveness.

To quantitatively validate that the rectangular geometry is better than its circular counterpart, a comparison experiment using the finite element method was conducted. All parameters of value were kept the same in both cases. Flange edges bonded to the piezoceramic are $4 \mathrm { m m }$ in width to ensure that they are firmly bonded together. The active dimension, barring flange edges, of the rectangular piezo plate is $1 5 \times 3 2$ $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ and that of the circular counterpart is $\phi 1 2 . 3 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , which means the overall area is $4 8 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ for both cases. Both the piezo plates and the bow-shaped plates are $0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ thick. In the simulation, the material properties of aluminum and PZT-$^ { 5 \mathrm { H } }$ are assigned to the bow-shaped plates and the piezo plates, respectively.

In the flex-compressive center, the piezoelectric element mainly works in the $^ { - 3 1 }$ mode. The polarization direction is parallel to the $z$ -axis and perpendicular to the stress direction. Therefore, the effective stress is in the $x$ direction (Cartesian coordinate system) for the rectangular flex-compressive center, and is in the radical direction (i.e. $\rho$ direction, cylindrical coordinate system) for the circular flex-compressive center. As shown in figures 4 and 5, it is noticeable that the effective stress in the rectangular one is much higher than that in the circular one. The average value of effective stress in the effective part is about $4 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { 7 }$ Pa for the rectangular transducer, and about $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 7 }$ Pa for the circular transducer. What is more, the rectangular transducer can generate $100 \%$ higher voltage than its circular counterpart (figure 6).

sections.heading: 3.1. Governing equations
sections.text:
One effective and simplified way to model the electromechanical system is to couple the electric effect into the mechanical vibration equation as an equivalent damping [24, 25]. However, this method assumes that the electrical damping is linearly proportional to the velocity, and therefore has a certain error. In this study, the electric dissipation is coupled as a separate term to get greater fidelity.

Although the electrical properties of piezoelectric materials are complex in practice, including resistive, capacitive, and inductive impedances [26], the capacitive impedance plays the dominant role under low-frequency excitations. Therefore, in this study, we neglect the effect of the inductive and resistive impedance, and model the piezoelectric element as an equivalent current source that is parallel-connected with an equivalent internal capacitance, as shown in figure 7. The PEH is connected to an external resistive load that, in conjunction with the equivalent capacitance of the piezoelectric element, consumes harvested mechanical energy from the base excitation. The electromechanical coupling system is defined by the following equations for the first resonant mode [27]

The nonlinearity of the system comes from the varying vibration amplitude, and can be modeled as an amplitudestiffened spring. Analytical expressions can visually articulate the relationship between different parameters so we can design and optimize the transducer more conveniently. Several approximate analytical solutions have been developed such as the straightforward expansion method, the elliptic perturbation method, and the harmonic balance method as concluded in [31] (p 127). sections.heading: 3.3. Nondimensional analysis
sections.text:
In this subsection, we study the nonlinear dynamic responses using the nondimensional solutions derived in the preceding subsection. Table 1 shows the parameters used in the analysis. The values correlate to the experimental prototype.

In the simulation, the tuning ratio, $\alpha$ , is set to be 1 to get the optimized power output. Since the tuning ratio varies along the excitation frequency, a dynamic-impedance matching circuit is indispensable for extracting optimum power from energy harvesters. Detailed information about the impedance matching technique is not in the scope of this paper, and interested readers should refer to [33, 34].

The effects of the linear and nonlinear damping are examined carefully. Figure 8 illustrates the frequency responses of the system with different damping ratios. Both linear and nonlinear damping have great influence on the mechanical response in the on-resonance region, but have little effect in the off-resonance region. As the damping increases, the nonlinear phenomena are restrained. The magnitude is decreased about 1/3 as the linear damping ratio increases from 0.005 to 0.04; it is about 1/5 for the nonlinear damping constant, which increases from 0.02 to 0.05. The damping also has different effects on the jump frequency. The jump-down frequency gets impaired notably as the damping increases. On the contrary, the jump-up frequency stays almost unchanged in the process. In the simulation, we found that the effect of damping on the electrical responses is similar to its effect on the mechanical responses. For brevity, we do not show the electrical responses here. Overall, the nonlinear damping has a considerable effect on both the mechanical and electrical responses, and should be taken into account.

Apart from the mechanical damping effect, the coupling effect is another energy-consuming term. It directly affects the power output and thus is of great significance for PEHs. Figure 9 exhibits mechanical and electrical responses with different coupling factors. Here, the coupling factor, $\kappa _ { : }$ represents how strong the mechanical domain is when coupled with the electrical domain. Unlike the damping effect, the effect of the coupling factor manifests differently for mechanical and electrical responses. When the coupling factor decreases from 0.22 to 0.10, the displacement amplitude of the vibration changes a little, while the voltage response is halved. This implies that for PEHs, different piezoelectric materials do not perform very distinctly mechanically, but have significantly different electrical responses. Thus, research that explores new materials with high piezoelectric coefficients is crucial to improving the efficiency of PEHs.

sections.heading: 4. Experiments
sections.text:
This section depicts the fabricated prototype and the experimental rig developed to characterize the performance of the HC-PEH. The active material used here was soft piezoceramic PZT- $^ { 5 \mathrm { H } }$ . The static capacitance, thickness coupling factor, and loss tan $\delta$ were measured to be $3 0 ~ \mathrm { n F }$ , 0.53, and 0.01, respectively. The effective volume of the PZT-5 H plate was $3 2 \times 1 5 \times \mathrm { ~ \ i ~ { ~ 2 ~ } ~ m m ^ { 3 } }$ . Table 2 demonstrates the values of the geometric and material parameters of the prototype. Figure 10 shows the experimental platform established to test the fabricated prototype. A small adjustable vise was used in the setup to fine tune the distance between the two fixed ends. The HC-PEH was mounted vertically on a electromagnetic shaker that supplied a harmonic excitation while operating. Experimental conditions were set via software interface on a PC and loaded to the controller. The controller regulated the vibration of the shaker via a signal amplifier based on the instructions from the PC and the feedback signal from an accelerometer (Kistler Instrument Corp.). A linear frequency sweep rate of $0 . 1 \mathrm { H z } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ was set throughout the experiment. The frequency sweep rate was small enough to avoid the interference from the excitation of adjacent frequencies. The electrical response voltage and the mechanical response velocity were monitored using an oscilloscope (Tektronix 3014) and a laser Doppler vibrometer (Polytec Inc. OFV-534), respectively. A $1 0 ~ M \varOmega$ high-impedance probe (Tektronix P6139B) was used in the system; the probe was much bigger than the matching impedance, and can be regarded as the open-circuit condition when no external resistance is connected in parallel. sections.heading: 5. Results and discussions
sections.text: In this section, we analyze the results from the simulations and experiments. The dynamic and electrical characteristics of the HC-PEH are examined. The performance of the HC-PEH prototype is also compared with current cutting-edge energy harvesters to verify its superiority over others.

sections.heading: 5.1. Dynamic and electrical characterization of the HC-PEH
sections.text:
An experiment was first conducted to find the optimal resistance. Figure 11 shows the measured voltage and power output as functions of external resistive loads. The potential difference between the two electrodes of the piezo plate increases as the resistive load increases, while the power output reaches its peak at $1 0 0 \mathrm { K } \Omega . ~ 1 0 0 \mathrm { K } \Omega$ is regarded as the optimal resistance and is used in experiments to extract maximum power.

![](images/424d9b271c64b2d8d920a51f317fe4019ffe26dee7d300fb28f5af166c984821.jpg)  
Figure 10. The experimental setup.

![](images/f97e3a039bf9d6056bcc46b235e81e5b3179aeb842635e660a0a5ae492e45ea2.jpg)  
Figure 11. Effect of the external resistance on the voltage and power responses of the HC-PEH under an excitation of $0 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ acceleration.

In most models developed for vibration-based energy harvesters, piezoelectric materials therein are assumed to obey the linear constitutive relations [35]. However, the linear assumption only works when piezoelectric materials bear weak loads. While large stress or voltage is applied, the response of the piezoceramics shows strong hysteresis and nonlinearity [36]. Consequently, piezoelectric coefficients, especially key parameters for energy harvesters such as charge constants $d _ { 3 1 } , d _ { 3 3 }$ and voltage constants $g _ { 3 1 } , \ g _ { 3 3 }$ , are no longer constant. In the HC-PEH, to achieve high power output, force is deliberately amplified greatly. Therefore, the effect of dynamic stress on the piezoelectric coefficients must be considered. Material experiments by Zhou et al [37] indicate that the compressive stress causes the piezoelectric charge constant, $d _ { 3 1 }$ , to increase approximately linearly before ${ 5 0 } \mathrm { M P a }$ for soft piezoceramics (see, in particular, figure 8 of [37]).

![](images/327c0f256f406b4073a6b09241a3a2444601effe6cbe5b7b0e422883bd7398c2.jpg)  
Figure 12. Effect of the nonlinear piezoelectricity on voltage responses of the HC-PEH. The blue dotted line is the simulation results with the nonlinear piezoelectric effect; the red dotted line is the simulation results with the linear piezoelectric effect. The green region represents upward-sweep experimental data; the yellow region denotes downward-sweep experimental data. It is connected with a resistor of $1 0 0 \mathrm { K } \varOmega$ under a $0 . 4 \ : \mathrm { g }$ excitation.

Based on the experimental data, the coupling factor $\theta$ herein, which corresponds to the piezoelectric charge constant, is assumed to be an approximate function of the mechanical displacement response

$$
\theta = k _ { \theta } X + \theta _ { 0 } ,
$$

where the slope, $k _ { \theta }$ , and constant term, $\theta _ { 0 }$ , are determined by fitting experimental data. $k _ { \theta } = 0 . 1 3$ $N / ( V \times m )$ ; $\theta _ { 0 } = 5 . 3 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ N / V$ .

![](images/4fa1a626063f27985f8149ae053c9bcd8c08b7232a6f47ab0e923f25ed664fb2.jpg)  
Figure 13. Comparison of velocity responses from simulations and experiments of the HC-PEH. The acceleration of the base excitation is: (a) $0 . 2 { \mathrm { g } }$ ; (b) $\mathrm { 0 . 3 } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { : }$ ; (c) $0 . 4 \ : \mathrm { g } \cdot$ ; (d) $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ . Dotted lines denote simulation results (blue dot: stable solution; red cross: unstable solution), and colored regions represent the data measured in experiments (green: upward frequency sweep; yellow: downward frequency sweep). It is under the open-circuit condition.

Figure 12 shows the effect of nonlinear piezoelectricity on the electrical response. The model that considers the nonlinear piezoelectric effect estimates the electrical responses accurately. In contrast, the model that only considers the linear piezoelectric effect underestimates the performance. It is intriguing and of great value to the development of PEHs to find that the piezoelectric performance can be ameliorated significantly by appropriate compressive stress. Exploiting the nonlinear piezoelectric effect may become a new tactic to improve the performance of PEHs.

Broadening the working bandwidth to adapt energy harvesters to the frequency-varying environment is currently an area of great interest. Figure 13 illustrates the velocity responses of the upward and downward frequency sweeps of the prototype in experiments and simulations under four different excitations. Nonlinear oscillations with distinct jump phenomena occur as the frequency of the excitation is swept forward and backward. The stronger the excitation is, the greater the responses are, and the wider the separations between the jump-up and jump-down points. Both jump-up and jump-down frequencies have a tendency to rise as the excitation increases. However, this tendency is only noticeable for the jump-down frequency that climbs from $2 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 5 . 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ as the excitation is boosted up from $0 . 2 { \mathrm { g } }$ to $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ , as shown in figure 13. As for the jump-up point, where the oscillation jumps from the low-energy orbit state to the highenergy orbit state, the increase is trivial $( 1 8 - 1 9 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ in simulation). The jump-up frequency, unlike its jump-down counterpart, is not stable either. In experiments, the jump-up frequency was tested many times. It changed around $1 9 \mathrm { H z }$ and showed a tendency to rise as the acceleration rose.

For comparison, both analytical results and experimental data are drawn in one figure for each acceleration level (figure 13). Qualitatively, under all different excitations, the analytical results agree very well with the experimental observations, no matter the on-resonance response, off-resonance response, or jump frequency. Quantitatively, the error of the maximum velocity response is under $5 \%$ for all conditions. It is concluded that the developed analytical model estimates the mechanical response of the HC-PEH accurately.

An effective model for PEHs should not only simulate the mechanical response, but more importantly, it should precisely estimate the electrical response. The capability of modeling the voltage response is examined and graphically indicated in figure 14. It is observed that, on the whole, the simulation shows good agreement with experimental measurements at different accelerations over the whole frequency spectra. As the excitation strength rises, the response amplitude, the bandwidth, and the jump frequency become bigger, wider, and higher, respectively.

![](images/d5a1a0954f3b5e7f8360539d288f57bd62ee1e708ea18288943f84f52c2f94ec.jpg)  
Figure 14. Comparison of voltage responses from simulations and experiments of the HC-PEH. The acceleration of the base excitation is: (a) $0 . 2 { \mathrm { g } }$ ; (b) $\mathrm { 0 . 3 } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { : }$ ; (c) $0 . 4 \ : \mathrm { g } \cdot$ ; (d) $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ . Dotted lines denote simulation results (blue dot: stable solution; red cross: unstable solution), and colored regions represent the data measured in experiments (green: upward frequency sweep; yellow: downward frequency sweep). The external resistance is $1 0 0 \mathrm { K } \varOmega$ .

The broader bandwidth benefits from the existence of nonlinearity in the system, which drives the peaks of the responses to lean toward higher frequencies. Since there is no consensus definition of bandwidth among the published works on energy harvesters and the classical half-power bandwidth definition is not a fair metric for asymmetric nonlinear response [38], we herein use a fixed-power bandwidth as a more practical metric from an engineering point of view. The fixed power is determined by the application. It is known that the power consumption of most of wireless sensors is $1 \mu \mathrm { { W } { - } 1 \mathrm { { m W } } }$ ; thus $1 \mathrm { m W }$ -bandwidth is used here. The bandwidth for the prototype is about $1 2 \mathrm { H z }$ under an excitation of $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ .

The frequency responses of the power output are omitted here because they have the same characteristics as the voltage response and can be calculated easily via equation (16). The maximum power outputs are $2 0 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ , $3 0 . 6 \mathrm { m W }$ , $4 4 . 0 \mathrm { m W }$ , and $5 4 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ under $0 . 2 \mathrm { g } , 0 . 3 \mathrm { g } , 0 . 4 \mathrm { g }$ , and $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ excitations, respectively.

Note that, unlike linear PEHs, two stable solutions may coexist over a certain frequency spectrum depending on the excitation strength. Take figure 14(b) for example; under the condition of $2 2 \mathrm { H z }$ frequency, $0 . 3 \mathrm { g }$ acceleration, the velocity response amplitude is $0 . 5 5 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ for the high-energy attractor, and $0 . 0 4 \mathrm { { m s } ^ { - 1 } }$ for the low-energy attractor. Whether highenergy or low-energy state physical responses is determined by the initial conditions and can be expounded by the domains of attractions [31, 39]. For vibration-based energy harvesters, obviously we prefer that the electrical response stays in high-energy branch to get higher energy output. Hence, practicable strategies to ensure the constant manifestation of the high-energy attractor are of great significance and worthy of further study.

![](images/cfb39871cf30102749b97c068365a6833cca72991138641262a9621f10463539.jpg)  
Figure 15. Effect of the electrical load on the mechanical response. (a) Simulation results; (b) open-circuit experimental data; (c) $1 0 0 \mathrm { K } \varOmega$ experimental data; (d) short-circuit experimental data. The vertical axis represents the absolute velocity of the flex-compressive center. The acceleration of the base excitation is $0 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ .

The reverse effect of the electrical load on the mechanical response of the electromechanical coupling system is studied, too. Three representative conditions—open-circuit, short-circuit, and impedance matching—are examined, as shown in figure 15. On the whole, the reverse effect is not pronounced. Specifically, we found that the velocity response is not attenuated consistently as the external resistance is reduced, but reaches a minimum at the impedance-matching condition. It is deemed that the phenomenon is caused by the electrical damping effect that extracts a portion of mechanical energy from the system. For the electromechanical coupling system, the overall damping is bigger with an optimal resistance than that of the open circuit and short circuit.

sections.heading: 5.2. Performance comparison
sections.text:
Currently, there is no general standard to compare different designs and approaches of vibration-based energy harvesters, and a variety of performance metrics have been proposed. The commonly used metric is the power density, which is defined as power output over volume. However, the overall power output is not always proportional to the volume, especially for some complex, nonlinear energy harvesters. The simplified calculation by Marin et al [40] suggested that the averaged power flow was proportional to volume4 3. More importantly, the power density does not take the most influential effect from the input excitation into account. Another widely adopted metric is efficiency. It is defined as output power over input power and is derived to be a function of the quality factor and the coupling factor [41]. However, the efficiency considers the effect of input excitation, but neglects the effect of the dimension. Besides, high efficiency does not always mean high power output for an electromechanical system in practice. The defined efficiency is useful when choosing active materials, but cannot predict whether the strategies for trapping energy are good or not. Roundy [42] enhanced the concept of efficiency and proposed a new metric effectiveness that considers the quality factor, density, coupling coefficient, and transmission coefficient of energy harvesters. However, coefficients in the defined effectiveness are dependent on operating conditions, and the operability of the effectiveness is poor. Several complicated performance metrics [43–45] also exist that take more parameters into consideration. They all are derived based on the specific linear SDOF structure and do not possess universality for different energy harvesters. Table 3. There is no universal performance metric because the performance of these energy harvesters is highly dependent on the operation conditions, dimensions, and materials employed. Different energy harvesters are developed for different vibration conditions. It is impractical and inappropriate to compare various designs and approaches with one benchmark. Authors believe that if the proposed energy harvester can meet the requirements of the application under specific constraints, then that is a suitable metric for evaluating different energy harvesters. Hence, parameters important to the end users, such as total power output, frequency, volume, and input excitation, should be listed. Table 3 shows a performance comparison between the proposed high-efficiency compressive-mode energy harvester and other state-of-the art models. The figure of merit normalized power density (NPD) $\left( \frac { \mathrm { P o w e r } } { \mathrm { V o l u m e } \times \mathrm { A c c e l e r a t i o n } ^ { 2 } } \right)$ [46] is added in the table. It is not a universal metric, but it gives us a general concept of the performance. Note that here, the volume refers to the volume of active materials. The entire volume is not advised for use in the calculations because the ways to measure the entire volume are not same, and accurate information is not always clearly documented in the literature. Besides, good deployments—for example, those using rectification and storage circuits as the seismic mass block—can significantly decrease the total volume. Generally, a PEH generates several microwatts to several hundred microwatts of power. Typical high-efficiency PEHs reported recently, as listed in table 3, can reach the level of several milliwatts. The HC-PEH prototype has a maximum power output of $5 4 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ , which is about two orders of magnitude over that of traditional PEHs and one order of magnitude over that of state-of-the-art PEHs under the same conditions. It is a landmark progress toward developing autonomous systems by harnessing ambient wasted energy. The HC-PEH also excels in terms of the power density and the NPD. The performance of the HC-PEH can be improved further by optimizing the structure parameters and using better materials (e.g., a single crystal).

sections.heading: 6. Summary
sections.text: In conclusion, an innovative energy harvester called a highefficiency compressive-mode piezoelectric energy harvester (HC-PEH) is studied theoretically and experimentally. An analytical model is developed and experimentally validated. It is found that when the excitation increases, a linear damping term is not capable of curbing the increase of the responses. The nonlinear damping effect must be considered carefully in the models of energy harvesters based on specific conditions. Meanwhile, it is noted that the piezoelectric effect also shows great nonlinearity in the experiments. This nonlinear effect comes from the induced high stress and is conducive to performance improvement. Exploiting piezoelectric nonlinearity may become a new tactic for improving performance of PEHs. A prototype (entire volume: $1 \bar { 2 } . 7 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ ; piezoelectric volume: $0 . 3 3 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ is fabricated and generates a maximum power of $5 4 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ under a harmonic excitation of $0 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ , which significantly outperforms current energy harvesters. The HC-PEH also shows distinct hardening nonlinearity and a broad working bandwidth at low-frequency spectra, which renders it more adaptable to the frequency-variant environment.
